Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Federal regulators announced $7.1 million in fines against American Airlines on Thursday over maintenance issues and problems with its drug- and alcohol-testing programs. American Airlines was fined for allowing aircrafts to fly while they knew they needed repairs. "The FAA believes the large total amount of the fine for these violations is appropriate because American Airlines was aware that appropriate repairs were needed, and instead deferred maintenance," the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement announcing the decision. "In intentionally continuing to fly the aircraft, the carrier did not follow important safety regulations intended to protect passengers and crew." American can still appeal the fines, the FAA said. The FAA also found the airline maintained inadequate drug- and alcohol-testing programs and failed to inspect safety lighting on a "timely" basis. The Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier said Thursday evening that it disagreed with the findings and called the penalties "excessive." "In accordance with FAA procedures for handling these matters, we have requested to meet with the FAA after we have had time to thoroughly review their findings, so that we may discuss the issues," the airline said in a written statement. "Since these matters are ongoing with the FAA, we will not have any further comment at this time." Nearly $4.5 million of the proposed fines stem from American's continued operation of two MD-83 jetliners in December 2007 after pilots reported problems with the autopilot systems, the FAA said. The two planes were flown a combined 58 times before the problems were corrected -- and one flew 10 times after an FAA inspector notified the airline that it had wrongly deferred needed repairs. In one incident, the autopilot disconnected during a landing on December 21, the FAA said. "American technicians did not check for the actual problem, and instead deferred maintenance using an inappropriate MEL (minimum equipment list) item. The plane flew another 36 passenger-carrying flights during December 21-31." The problem was later traced to a piece of radio gear separate from the autopilot, the FAA said. Meanwhile, a different MD-83 flew four flights without a fully functioning autopilot after American mechanics put off repairs.  Regulators also accuse American of operating planes without timely inspections of their emergency lighting systems. In April, American canceled more than 3,000 flights to conduct inspections of wiring bundles in wheel wells of its 300 MD-80 jets, snarling air traffic for five days. The FAA ordered American and several other airlines to examine the wiring, which had the potential to start fires or cause landing gear to malfunction.

(CNN) — Federal regulators on Thursday announced $7.1 million in fines against American Airlines over maintenance issues and deficiencies in its drug- and alcohol-testing programs.

American Airlines was fined for allowing aircraft to operate despite knowing they required repairs.

“The FAA believes the large total amount of the fine for these violations is appropriate because American Airlines was aware that appropriate repairs were needed, and instead deferred maintenance,” the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement announcing the decision. “In intentionally continuing to fly the aircraft, the carrier did not follow important safety regulations intended to protect passengers and crew.”

The FAA said American Airlines may still appeal the fines.

The agency also found that the airline maintained inadequate drug- and alcohol-testing programs and failed to inspect safety lighting on a “timely” basis.

The Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier said Thursday evening that it disagreed with the findings and described the penalties as “excessive.”

“In accordance with FAA procedures for handling these matters, we have requested to meet with the FAA after we have had time to thoroughly review their findings, so that we may discuss the issues,” the airline said in a written statement. “Since these matters are ongoing with the FAA, we will not have any further comment at this time.”

Nearly $4.5 million of the proposed fines stem from American’s continued operation of two MD-83 jetliners in December 2007 after pilots reported problems with the autopilot systems, the FAA said.

The two aircraft were flown a combined 58 times before the problems were corrected—and one flew 10 times after an FAA inspector notified the airline that it had improperly deferred necessary repairs.

In one incident, the autopilot disconnected during a landing on December 21, the FAA said.

“American technicians did not check for the actual problem, and instead deferred maintenance using an inappropriate MEL (minimum equipment list) item. The plane flew another 36 passenger-carrying flights during December 21-31.”

The problem was later traced to a piece of radio equipment separate from the autopilot, the FAA said.

Meanwhile, a different MD-83 operated four flights without a fully functioning autopilot after American mechanics postponed repairs.

Regulators also accused American of operating aircraft without timely inspections of their emergency lighting systems.

In April, American canceled more than 3,000 flights to conduct inspections of wiring bundles in the wheel wells of its 300 MD-80 jets, disrupting air traffic for five days. The FAA had ordered American and several other airlines to inspect the wiring, which had the potential to start fires or cause landing gear to malfunction.

Federal regulators said Thursday that American Airlines faces $7.1 million in proposed penalties related to aircraft maintenance violations and shortcomings in its drug and alcohol testing programs.

The FAA said the airline permitted planes to keep flying even though it knew repairs were required. In announcing the penalties, the Federal Aviation Administration said the size of the fine was justified because American Airlines had been aware that proper repairs were necessary but chose to postpone the work. The agency added that by deliberately continuing to operate the aircraft, the airline failed to comply with key safety rules designed to protect passengers and crew members.

According to the FAA, American Airlines still has the right to appeal the fines.

The agency also said American’s drug and alcohol testing programs were insufficient and that the airline did not inspect safety lighting systems within the required timeframe.

The airline, which is based in Fort Worth, Texas, said Thursday evening that it disagreed with the FAA’s conclusions and described the penalties as “excessive.” In a written statement, American said it had asked to meet with the FAA under the agency’s procedures after reviewing the findings in detail, so the two sides could discuss the issues. The company also said that because the matters were still pending with the FAA, it would not comment further at that time.

Almost $4.5 million of the proposed fines involve American’s continued use of two MD-83 aircraft in December 2007 after pilots reported autopilot problems, the FAA said. The two jets were flown a total of 58 times before the issues were fixed. One of them flew 10 times after an FAA inspector told the airline that it had improperly delayed needed repairs.

In one case, the FAA said, the autopilot shut off during a landing on December 21. The agency said American’s technicians did not investigate the real cause of the malfunction and instead postponed maintenance by relying on an improper minimum equipment list item. That aircraft then made 36 more passenger flights between December 21 and December 31.

The FAA later determined that the problem was connected to a separate piece of radio equipment, not the autopilot itself.

In another case, a different MD-83 made four flights without a fully working autopilot after American mechanics delayed repairs, regulators said.

The FAA also alleged that American operated aircraft without inspecting their emergency lighting systems on time.

Earlier in April, American canceled more than 3,000 flights so it could inspect wiring bundles in the wheel wells of its 300 MD-80 aircraft, disrupting air travel for five days. The FAA had directed American and several other airlines to check the wiring because it could potentially cause fires or interfere with landing gear operation.

**FAA fines American Airlines $7.1 million over maintenance, testing violations**

The Federal Aviation Administration has proposed $7.1 million in civil penalties against American Airlines, accusing the carrier of violating federal safety rules involving aircraft maintenance, employee drug and alcohol testing, and delayed repairs on MD-83 aircraft.

The largest portion of the penalties stems from allegations that American operated McDonnell Douglas MD-83 aircraft after required repairs had been improperly deferred or not completed within mandated time limits, according to the FAA. The agency said the airline failed to comply with maintenance procedures designed to ensure aircraft are airworthy before returning to service.

The FAA also cited American for problems with its drug and alcohol testing program, alleging that the airline failed to properly conduct required testing for employees in safety-sensitive positions. Federal rules require carriers to maintain strict testing programs for workers such as mechanics, pilots and others whose duties can affect flight safety.

In addition, the FAA accused American of broader maintenance violations, including failures to follow required inspection and repair procedures.

The airline has a period of time to respond to the FAA’s allegations before the penalties become final. Civil penalties proposed by the FAA are often subject to negotiation, and airlines may challenge the findings or seek reductions.

American Airlines has previously said it takes safety and regulatory compliance seriously and works closely with federal regulators to address concerns.

The MD-83, part of the McDonnell Douglas MD-80 series, was once a major part of American’s domestic fleet but has since been retired. The aircraft type was widely used by U.S. carriers for short- and medium-haul routes before being phased out in favor of newer, more fuel-efficient jets.

The FAA said the enforcement action underscores the agency’s focus on ensuring that airlines follow maintenance rules and maintain required safety oversight programs.

The FAA said the alleged violations reflected failures in maintenance oversight and compliance systems, not merely paperwork errors.
